title: Ukrainian NGO head says Russian attacks on infrastructure are a sign of desperation
html:
Taras Chmut, head of a Ukrainian military support organization, in Toronto on Tuesday. He says Russia is increasingly targeting Ukraine's critical infrastructure as both sides struggle to make advances on the battlefield.Arlyn McAdorey/The Globe and Mail

Taras Chmut, the head of a Ukrainian military support organization, says that because Russia has failed to make any significant advances along the front lines, it has brought its war against Ukraine to its infrastructure, targeting bridges so crucial to logistics that it could make the country nearly uninhabitable.

Mr. Chmut, who leads Come Back Alive, an NGO that provides the Ukrainian army with equipment and supplies and runs educational and training initiatives, believes the Russian military’s desperation has led it to exploit Kyiv’s dwindling air defences.

“That’s the primary thing right now – targeting bridges and logistics. We believe the battlefield as such is now becoming a secondary thing,” Mr. Chmut said in an interview in Toronto.

He argues that military technology has developed so exponentially that it’s been hard for the Russian military to advance – and equally hard for the Ukrainian army to liberate its occupied regions.

“None of the sides can really progress,” he said. “Both sides are looking for alternatives and what are the other domains, how can we impact each other. So logistics is one of those that Russia is exploiting right now, and they are terrorizing the whole society, making the country being almost unlivable.”

Overnight Monday, Russia struck two of Kyiv’s main bridges over the Dnipro River with seven ballistic missiles. Both bridges are crucial for residents who need to travel from one side of the city to the other. The same night, Ukraine struck the Kerch Bridge that connects Russia with occupied Crimea.

While the bridges in Kyiv are far from the front lines, targeting them is yet another aspect of the war, Mr. Chmut said. Taking them out affects logistics and “slows down” the whole country. And the aftermath of attacks on infrastructure, whether it’s bridges or the power grid, is particularly harsh during the winter − and Ukrainians are bracing for another bad one.

“It’s hard for Ukrainians, obviously, because we have to survive and go through the winter somehow,” he said.

Mr. Chmut said that while in Canada he has attended fundraising events. His NGO is raising money to buy unmanned ground vehicles, which can help retrieve wounded soldiers and also transport supplies such as food and medicine to front line areas.

He also met with officials in Ottawa. He said the Canadian government has agreed to support his organization’s initiatives, which involve developing military training infrastructure, but could not provide further details. Global Affairs Canada did not respond to questions about its support from The Globe.

Mr. Chmut mentioned that both armies were looking for alternative ways to continue the fight – as evidenced by Ukraine’s strikes on the Kerch Bridge. The bridge is not only a crucial supply route for the Russian army; it’s of strategic and symbolic importance to Russian President Vladimir Putin. For Ukrainians, though, it’s a painful reminder of Russian occupation.

In a post on X Tuesday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called it an “unprecedented operation in response to Russian strikes on our infrastructure.”

“Russia strikes our infrastructure every day, including bridges in Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro, Kyiv, and the Odesa region. We are restoring our infrastructure. But we are also reminding Russia that war will always return to where it began. Ukraine’s defensive capabilities are strong and will remain so, and we will never leave terror against our cities and people unanswered,” he wrote.

In a later post, he said Ukrainian-made weapons had hit the bridge to Crimea, adding, “This is how our defense sector is developing.”

Mr. Chmut said that while Ukraine is manufacturing a lot of its own weapons, it is running out of air-defence missiles.

“We can count them in pieces how much Ukraine is getting week by week,” he said.

“What we see right now is that Russia is actively destroying the world order – and as soon as it is destroyed, that means that any bigger or more powerful country can invade the weaker one,” he said. “Your country is also under threat here.”

U.S. President Donald Trump recently said in an interview with 60 Minutes that the shape of Ukraine would change as a result of negotiations with Russia.

Mr. Chmut said Ukrainians are “not really big fans” of that idea.

“Imagine yourself, you’re living in your apartment, and then your neighbour comes and says the living room is now mine and no one in this world can do anything, or doesn’t want to,” he said, noting that Ukraine gave up its nuclear weapons after the collapse of the Soviet Union in exchange for security assurances from the U.S., Britain and Russia.

“If agreements mean nothing, then there’s something wrong with this world.”

With a report from the Associated Press
summary: Unable to make any progress on the battlefield, Moscow is increasingly hitting civilian targets
